text: 2 Weeks in Korea. Hey guys, I just came from a 2 week trip to South Korea. This isn't the first time I've been but it's the first time as an independent adult that I've gone. After this trip, I've definitely learned to appreciate just how cool Korea is. For such a small country, there's so much history and culture jammed packed into it. I spent the first week in Seoul and then the last week in Busan and Jeju Island before going back to Seoul for a couple of days. I used to go to Korea as a kid for my summer breaks and it was always two months (June/July in Seoul). To be honest, as a kid, I hated it. It was hot, I barely spoke enough Korean at the time to leave our family's apartment to buy snacks and food, let alone use public transit. As an adult, I've come to really love Seoul for all its quirks and its especially how unique each of Seoul's neighborhoods are. If I could go back, I'd probably spend more days in Busan to be honest. I felt like I rushed through the popular tourist-y things to do there without really diving into the city. Jeju was refreshing to me. It wasn't the hustle and bustle of a giant city like Seoul and it reminded me that a slower pace to life exists in Korea. I rented a car in Jeju and it was nice to just drive along the coast without worrying about being on time for the next train or bus. Hope you guys like these photos, cheers!
label: trip_report

text: A day in Verona. Yesterday I finally had the opportunity to visit Verona, which has been a dream of mine for years, safe to say it did not dissapoint! I was lucky enough to have a beautiful sunny day (rare for northern Italy in november), so aside from the stunning Basilica of sant Anastasia I just walked around outside. The city reminds me so much of Venice on land, just with more Roman ruins. It's very interesting to experience a roman city grid that has been perserved for 2 millenia, but with a more medieval-renessaince vibe. I skipped Juliet's balcony as I had no interest lol. In the morning it was quiet but by the late afternoon it got crowded on via Mazzini to Ponte Pietra, but unlike Firenze or Venezia it didn't feel chocked, and if you turn to any side street it's empty. For the sunset I walked up to castel San Pietro, clearly a very popular spot as it was crowded but the view of the old town on the river bend with it's soaring towers and glowing red roofs was very worth it. Verona is a very authentically romantic and gorgeous city if you skip the Romeo and Juliet scams, it felt like a mix of multiple cities to me but unique and true to itself.
label: trip_report

text: Switzerland - 10 days in a fairy tale. We've been wanting to visit Switzerland for a while now but put it off for years due to the perceived cost. But with the ever rising Swiss Franc and rampant global inflation I decided to just bite the bullet and go this past October combining it with a trip to Lake Como in Italy. Glad I finally did since it was an absolute delight to for the eyes. Even coming from a very mountainous part of the world, the Swiss landscape evokes a fairy tale like atmosphere with soaring peaks, grasslands, and farmhouses all in one photo shot. And before anyone asks, yes it was even more expensive than I had feared. It’s the only place I've been where restaurants regularly charge you for tap water - insanity! Our itinerary consisted of: Lucerne - The town itself was nice but overtouristed like many European towns. Good to spend a couple days wandering it's streets but head up to the Alps, that's why you're here! Pilatus - Great day trip from Lucerne and intro to the Alps. We did the Golden circle which consists of a bus ride, cable car, cogwheel railway, and boat ride. Hike over to Mt. Tomlishorn for another fantastic view. Lake Brienz - Took a boat ride from Interlaken to the small town of Iseltwald (which is popular with fans of a particular K-drama). The water was impossibly florescent blue and the town is about as cute and quaint as you can imagine. Lauterbrunnen Valley - We based ourselves in Wengen which was perfect as it was central enough to visit many other towns in the area - Lauterbrunnen, Grindelwald, Jungfraujoch. The views are breathtaking basically everywhere you go. If there's one place you need to visit in Switzerland it's here. Kleine Scheidegg to Männlichen is an easy yet gorgeous hike. Jungfraujoch - I didn't love as it was super pricey and touristy . They really try and pack everyone in so go early. A lot of people from warm countries come up to experience snow year round but being from Canada the novelty was kind of lost to us. Still, the ride up on the highest railway in Europe is impressive. If only we had such infrastructure in Canada! Lake Thun - Rainy day for us so it didn't look as great as Lake Brienz, but we had a quick stop off in the town of Speiz which had a cool castle to visit. Zermatt/Matterhorn - Wow. words can't really describe your first view of such an icon. Was setting myself up for disappointment seeing it was overcast, but taking the Gornergrat railway up to a neighbouring peak gives you amazing views. Don't miss the short hike to the Riflesee lake to see it reflected in all it's glory. Bern - the capital is really quite nice and I dare say I enjoyed this urban experience the most in the country. It looks like something out of a storybook and isn't completely overrun with tourists Zurich - Had to come for the airport but we had a decent time. It wasn't as soulless as many people have described but it is one of the cleanest cities I've seen. There's a very nice old town to while away a day or two.
label: trip_report

text: Algerian Sahara. I got back from a remarkable 7 day camping trip to the deep south of Algeria (around Djanet). I first “discovered” this as a good adventure option given its relatively off-the-beaten track nature and my curiosity of the Sahara desert and its cultures. Tours deep into the south of Algeria all require a guide (typically a duo consisting of a guide/cook and a driver). They can be found using websites such as Getyourguide or TourHQ. I chose the latter - it works by you putting up a tour request, and tour agencies will try to offer you an itinerary and the price. Note that the offers I got were all from agencies based in the north of the country, who act as middlemen with local tour operators (guides and drivers). A relatively young tour agency offered me a private 7 day trip (one of my key needs to maximise flexibility) for a fairly good price of 1550 USD, excluding flights. Expect a much lower price per person accordingly if you are thinking of doing a group tour. The trip (most of these locations can be searched on Google Maps): -Day 1: Flight to Djanet via Algiers, arriving in the early hours I met my driver (spoke French only), who took me to a local guesthouse for some rest. Around midday I met up with the driver and the guide/cook (English speaking), went for lunch at Djanet town, stocked up and headed to the desert. The first camp spot were the Erg Admer sand dunes just outside Djanet. -Day 2: Erg Admer northwest to the highlands of Tassili N’Ajjer National Park, with stops at the Assar oasis and the petroglyphs at Tin Taghirt. Camping near Tin Taghirt. -Day 3: Tin Taghirt northwest to the oasis settlement of Iherir and the abandoned nomad base of Idaren. Then further west to the campsite among the rock formations of Tasset. -Day 4: Tasset back south to another part of Erg Admer for some more dune camping. -Day 5: Erg Admer north to the canyons and oasis of Essendilene, then further east to the campsite in the rock formations of Tikoubaouine. -Day 6: Tikoubaouine back to Djanet via the Crying cow rock engravings. Souvenir buying in Djanet market, dinner then back to hotel. -Day 7 (early hours): Flight out of Djanet to Algiers. Conditions: -Camp conditions are adequate, the food was clean, freshly made (usually stews and soups with canned tuna or beef or chicken) and I did not get sick from anything. No toilets provided so I had to do my deeds in the open. Tent was basic and did make noise when it got windy. Sleeping mattress was also basic (and inevitably dusty). -Weather in November: still very dry and hot during day time, around 32C in the shade. It was quite draining, literally. Night times on the other hand got cold (10 or so C). -Road conditions: very good on the paved N3 main road. Gravel/sand a bit more bumpy but bearable. -The flies were relentless, even in the middle of the dunes. They cling onto you much unlike what I have encountered. There were also mosquitoes in the oases, but my guide reassured me no malaria risk. The good: -I saw a LOT, the Sahara is much more than dunes. I saw canyons, highlands that have an uncanny resemblance to Iceland, oases, dramatic rock formations. It just kept on giving. -The Tuareg culture is vibrant, my driver and guide were both keen to show it to me, including tea ceremonies for each meal. The less good: -Air Algérie, the national (monopolised) carrier. It was BAD, 3 of the 4 flights were delayed, all of them by over 2 hrs. Plane interiors were in a dreadful state. -The initial itinerary planning and communication - I realised on Day 1 the final itinerary was different from that proposed by the agency (including Tin Merzouga, large red coloured sand dunes further to the south of Djanet, which is where most tourists go, and where I anticipated to visit). I let it slip given that I nevertheless enjoyed the tour very much. The Algiers-based agency is very young (mine was first trip they tried to organise in the Djanet region), and the organiser was friendly, helpful and communicative (I met him when I arrived in Algiers airport). Other notes: -I barely saw any other tourists given that the route we took is less popular than the Tadrart Rouge one. -USD/EUR can be exchanged to DZD informally in the black market, but at bad rates. I never used my bank card at all during the trip. -eSIM works mostly in Djanet and the larger settlement stops, but otherwise the desert is signal-dead, as expected. -Visas: most nationalities require a Visa, which is an extra cost (100 or so USD). -A deposit is paid upon tour agreement on TourHQ, I then gave the remainder USD to the organiser when I met him in Algiers.
label: trip_report

text: “Poor Niagara” said Roosevelt when seeing Iguazu Falls. November 8-9, 2026 And I have to admit the First Lady had a point. The Iguazu Falls are an absolutely massive and spectacular sight, so big it’s hard to wrap your head around - most impressively, it’s not “a” fall, but a collection of 200+ falls, stretching for 1.7 miles. To properly visit them you need 2 full days, one for the Argentinian and one for the Brazilian side. And while crossing the borders can definitely be quite confusing, local buses and/or taxis make the process definitely doable. The Devil’s Throat was unfortunately closed on the Argentinian side during my visit, but the Brazilian one was open and I feel like ultimately I got the experience I came for - and got absolutely soaked. And then I wasn’t sure about visiting Parque del Aves, bird sanctuary, but in the end feel like it was well worth it, for the parrots and toucans if nothing else. Definitely can recommend, especially in sunny weather. Just watch out for the raccoons (coatis), they will try to steal your food. Photos: 1,2 9-13 Brazilian side of Iguazu Falls 3-8, 14, Argentinian side of Iguazu Falls 15,16 Parque das Aves in Brazi 17 Hito Tres Fronteras (Argentina) 18 Mirador Escondido in Puerto Iguazu
label: trip_report

text: The Argentinian side is much better. If you have time I would recommend (I had to google it) "sendero Macuco". It is supposedly forbidden to get into the water, but when I was there there were only 2 other people (I went early in the morning a 2nd day in the Argentinian side) so I went it (the fall is inside a pond so it is not dangerous). So cool. If you are only 1 day in the Argentinian side it is not worth it, but spending more time it is worth. Devil’s Throat is undoubtedly the most impressive natural place I have ever been. text: Wildlife - The best national parks are in central Sumatra. You can see monkeys, elephants, Orang-Utans if you're lucky. Tigers are there too, but no chance you'll see one. Exotic fruit - Everywhere. Views - Mount Bromo I guess. A few other mountains on Java work too but be aware of volcanic activity and weather conditions. It's not a leisure walk. Good eats - Indonesian food is great basically everywhere. Beach - The beaches are generally good. I recommend Yogyakarta overall, it's definitely fun and friendly.
label: advice

text: You might want to indicate more information where you are from next time. Like as a Singaporean, dragon fruit and rambutams are normal fruits to me but might be consider exotic for other cultures. 4 days isn't a lot of time for Indonesia if you wish for views, wildlife, food, exotic fruits, beaches. So you have to stick 1 region or prepare for a very packed itinerary. For wildlife, I highly recommend Borneo (Malaysia side might be easier) where you can spent time admiring elephants, gibbons, and orangutans. Or Komodo Island via a minimum 3 days boat trip, where you can spot Komodo dragons, giant mantra rays, and bats. In addition, I notice you are an Australian (I assumed), so rambutam, dragon fruits, mangosteen, and papaya are common in these regions as well.
label: advice

text: Hey guys. I've been traveling for 11 months and, honestly, I feel kind of burnt out and want to rant a tad. I'm 23 and I saved for many years to be able to travel extensively after graduating university. It's something I thought about on a regular basis for a very long time. Still, I felt I always kept a very open mind and never had specific expectations. In the past year I've done some slow traveling like spending 3 months in Spain and 3 months in Morocco. I've also done some very fast traveling like spending one night in Glasgow, or two nights in London, or two nights in Cork. I've done some medium speed as well like two weeks in Dublin, two weeks in Belfast, one week in Amsterdam, or a week in Poznán. I've decided I really don't like the fast travel. It makes me so tired and I take in a lot less. I feel like I have a list and I'm just checking things off instead of actually being there and getting to know it. I also like to make friends along the way but that's mostly happened only when I stay somewhere for more than two weeks. I've been doing some volunteering along the way which helps meet people and experience the surroundings. So, I'm running kind of low on money and I'm looking at a map of Europe. I have all the places I wanted to go marked. First of all, I won't be able to go to all those places - money went a lot faster than I anticipated last month (thanks UK). Second, even if I take away half those places, if I want to 'see' the rest of them, they will be really fast visits (3 month max in schengen). So, now, I'm considering just visiting a friend in Germany for a few weeks, then just flying (yes flying, as in skipping the hitch hiking) to Croatia where it's cheaper and hopefully not too cold yet, and just staying there for a month while planning my next move (hopefully Asia). I just feel like I'm really lacking enthusiasm lately, not to mention energy and money. I don't want to go home early though. I don't feel like I've...done it? Also, on a more personal thoughts level... I feel funny saying it but... I feel like I haven't even had my "grand adventure." I have a lot of stories that don't have climaxes. One time I had to chase down a bus so I wouldn't get stuck somewhere...heh heh, amazing right? I guess I was kind of expecting to have more awesome stories and adventures at this point. I go out. I meet locals. Sometimes I completely throw away my itinerary and just go with the flow. Where's the great adventure? When I tell people I've been traveling for so long they immediately want stories and I really can't think of anything too interesting. Have you felt this way before? How do I get past this mental block? Like I said, I don't want to just 'give up' but at the same time, traveling has kind of lost its sexiness for me at the moment. And yes, I've tried staying in and watching movies, talking to friends on skype, and just relaxing. I almost feel like I'm missing something. How can I get that spark?
label: rant

text: I haven't done anything long term like what you're doing, but I'm aware that I'm constantly looking for that spark as well. But then I remind myself that that's not what life's about - it's about the little things that are special only to you. Yes, there are occasionally the crazy stories, but they are only so memorable because they're so rare. A lot of times when I travel, I don't realize until a few days later that my fondest memories are the ones that made me smile like a dork for the longest time, whether it was a simple act of kindness or a conversation I had with someone. I can see where you're coming from though - if I had saved up and waited a long time for such a monumental trip, I would expect it to be filled with crazy awesome stories as well. Even back home though, my best adventures were all unexpected and I never have the mindset of expecting one. I know it's easier said than done, but maybe letting go of the awesome-story-worthy exceptions may lead you to some :). Don't worry about what other people think and what they want to hear. Your memory of your own experiences and what you felt will last exponentially longer than their memory of your stories.
label: advice

text: When you run out of money and have to go back to your day job, you will look back and wish you could be back at your present position, traveling again. Just enjoy it. Stop thinking about what it "should" be. Travel is different for everyone. It is dependent on the individual.

text: Glimpses of Amdo region, north west China. Far off the beaten path. Following on from my previous reports on travelling in China, this is a compilation of pics from the north west China, commonly known as Amdo, one of the three cultural and historic region of Tibet. It is home to about twenty five percent of Tibetan population. I had always wanted to dip my toes in the water of the Yellow River : China's Sorrow. Over the centuries, more people have died in flooding along the Yellow River than along all other world rivers combined. But it is also the river which has shaped the history of China. It is rightfully known as “The Mother River” as the vast fertile plane it created helped the population to grow and establish many large cities. We took a boat ride on the Yellow River passing by the "stone forest" to reach the Bing ling Si monastery with its massive Buddha statue. Another highlight was staying at a remote place called Gannan grassland, under the shadow of the white cliffs. Vast is an understatement in relation to Tibetan plateau. Visited several monasteries including the huge Labrang monastery with world's largest prayer wheel corridor and the dazzling Langmu si monastery, home to the Yellow Hat sect. We had a guide and driver. No special permit was needed. Ended the trip at Lanzou, home of the famous noodle.

text: Recently went on a similar roadtrip through Kham and Amdo, nice to see another foreigner visiting the Tibetan areas outside of the TAR. I wouldn’t describe Labrang, Lanzhou and Langmusi as “off the beaten path” though since they’re massively popular witg domestic tourists and even included in the english Lonely Planet. We started and ended in Chengdu, from where we drove to Lanzhou, Xining and then westwards to Yushu (with detours at Anye Maqin etc). From there it’s another 5-hour drive to Gaden Si and other small-scale monasteries in Nanqen county, very remote and hard to get to but very much worth it. Then we went back to Yushu, from where we entered the western part of Sichuan and slowly made our way back to Chengdu. Along the way we stopped at Serxu, Dzogchen monastery, Yulong Lhatso, Dege, Kathok, Yarchen Gar, Sertar and Lianbaoyeze. Dzogchen and Kathok were our favourites. Perhaps some inspiration for a follow-up trip, this time without a guide?:)

text: PSA and a Priceline Story: Always call and complain/question if something is not right! Hi all, I have a story to tell you about why you should always complain and question, if you feel something is not right (within reason, not for every little thing). TLDR: This was a situation that happened with Priceline, and after I called and questioned it, they offered a great resolution/compensation. My story: I booked a flight (for two) to Peru over Thanksgiving and I booked it on Priceline in “first” class on Interjet Airlines (I think just “Priority” in their term of classes – seat up front, check a bag, etc). When I got my confirmation number, I went to Interjet’s site and entered my number in, to make sure the ticket was issued without error after paying Priceline - and the ticket said the class was “Light” fare! Which means back of the plane seating and only a carry-on bag! Now, that alone is not a big deal to me, if I myself had chosen that class…because I usually only take a carry-on bag anyway (I hate checking bags!) and I don’t care where I sit on the plane as long as I am next to my travel companion and get to my destination. The issue was that the Priceline website was telling completely false information and I didn’t think that was right. First class down to the lowest class? Not cool. So I called Priceline and told them all this, not in a mean way, but definitely did show that I was frustrated and unimpressed with this incorrect information on their site and in my booking, and especially that I wouldn’t have even noticed if I didn’t go myself and check this on the Interjet site, outside of Priceline. They apologized and said they do see that there is a discrepancy in what it shows on my Priceline confirmation email after I paid (First) and what was booked for me by them (Light). They said they were escalating it to the supervisor level who would call Interjet to see what they can do and call me back later. They called back later that day and said Interjet can’t really do anything to get me into the upgraded class now that the flights are booked and it’s through a third-party site who can't make the changes themselves. When the Priceline rep said that, I was feeling like all hope was lost. But I persisted and asked how they could legally post one completely different class and then when the ticket is issued it’s the opposite of that class, and then say “tough luck” to the passenger. The rep said they understood my frustration and would escalate this further and call back again. I got the callback two days later and they said that because this was a discrepancy on their site, and they take responsibility for that, that they are refunding my whole flight price, but NOT canceling my tickets! So a completely free flight for two to Peru, just for speaking up that I noticed this difference. PHEW! So I just wanted to put that out in the travel world, that if there is a big problem or issue you notice, that you should always feel you can reach out to the airline or provider and ask for some sort of resolution, and persist if their answer isn’t the best the first time. You can't get anything resolved if you don't try. I didn’t expect quite as big of a resolution as I got ($800 flights to Peru for free, I was just expecting a slight refund on the price for the class difference) but I never would have known if I didn’t try!

text: A meandering rant of what I learned about hitchhiking from 3 Years of traveling. Alright, so here's what I know about hitchhiking. First thing is first you want to get to the main highways. You want to do this safely so you need to take some pretty basic elements, commonsense, reflective material, food, and water. Lots of water. We're talking pissing clear every three hours amount of water. The reason for all the water is because dehydration will cause you to pass out. And passing out near cars going 65 mph on average is not a good thing. Here's a gear list of what I took. ALICE frame pack size medium. This pack served me very well on freight and the road. It's light, it's tough and it's cheap. Usually you can pick up a used one for 40 bucks at Army Navy, if you can't find one cheap get a rucksack with long leads for the straps. You want to carry a ruck close to the small of your back and just above your tail bone, that will put most of the weight on your hips. If you can't set the straps so the bottom of the pack is resting on the top of your tail bone don't get it. You'll wear out your shoulders and cause backpain. Peanut butter, tortillas, crystal light flavoring packets, spam, beef jerkey. Try not to carry canned food as it is expensive and will not last you long. Also canned food is ungodly heavy. You can get all the fat you need for the day from one spoon full of peanut butter and tortillas have loads of lard which is full of carbohydrates. Because you will be walking miles on end for days you'll need as many calories as you can get. I usually took one or two cans of dollar store chili, would eat half of one for breakfast and snack on peanut butter and tortillas. One can of dollar store chili has 3000 calories so half a can in the morning should do you pretty good till lunch. Hopefully people who give you rides will also OFFER you food, I screamed offer because you should never ask for food or money. Never, fly a sign and never spange. You should instead busque, I juggled, blew fire, and rode a unicycle for my money if i couldn't find work elsewhere. On the road you'll meet many different travelers but more on this later. A good sleeping bag. You will want a cheap one that is synthetic and rated to 32 degrees. Get a 0 degree bag if you can. You want a synthetic bag because it's warm when it's wet. ALL sleeping bags get wet. It's unavoidable.You'll also want to pack socks, lots of socks. you can get by with 1 pair of underwear and one pair of pants but you'll end up blowing through 14 pairs of socks in a week trust me. Also take comfortable shoes, dont' take hiking boots as they are heavy and tend to make your feet sweat more than they should. Dry feet are happy feet. Take a 6ft by 8ft tarp. This is by far the best thing you can take, it'll water proof your gear, it'll get you out of the rain, it'll prevent you being bitten by fleas and ticks when you sleep in the field it is awesome. Take a lightweight thick paper back book. I always suggest V by Thomas Pynchon. You'll want the paper back because it weighs next to nothing compared to the hard cover. You can usually find this book at used bookstores for cheap because everybody wants to say they've read this book but few have ever had the time to make it all the way through. You will have time. You will have nothing but time. When you are at the Army Navy store also buy 3 P38 can openers, they'll try and sell you on the P51 dont' do it, the P51 is more likely to bend, trust me I know this for a heart rendering fact. One bent on me and all I had to open cans was an old flattened spoon I had found on the ground. Take a Bic lighter with you. Many people who offer you rides also smoke and many of these people for some inexplicable reason never have a lighter. Also if somebody offers you a joint and you don't feel comfortable smoking it don't. If somebody offers you booze from a bottle wipe off the rim, put it to your lips and make a tight seal against your closed lips. Tilt the bottle back quickly and then down quickly. That's how you fake a swallow, it's an old hobo trick taught to everybody who ever traveled as a kid. It's so you don't ever get as drunk as the guy passing the bottle. You don't ever want to be as drunk as that guy. It can lead to bad things. Also if a person is obviously drunk that's picked you up, and this will happen more than you want it to, politely ask to be let off at the next exit. Then walk out of sight of the driver, wait for them to drive off and get back on the highway and stick your thumb back out. Believe me you don't want to be in the car when that guy gets arrested and is put through a sobriety test. The cop will not look kindly on you. Spent 2 weeks in county because of a drunk asshole in Alabama. Ok now to the people you will meet. They will be awesome, and terrible. Kind and frightening. Compassionate, and apathetic. They'll give you so much faith in humanity, and show you how evil the normal person can be. Don't ever agree to something you don't feel comfortable with. Always agree with the tirade if the person is driving. Always agree with the driver. If you see a group of people sleeping, sleep atleast 100 yards from them, unless you are in a city. If you're in a city sleep on the roof of the nearest abandoned building you can find. For some reason crackheads are afraid of heights. More on roof sleeping later. Never share a needle, never carry narcotics or paraphernalia. The travelers you will meet that are your age can fall into two distinct categories, people you can travel with and people you can't. Anybody over 30 and traveling avoid. The hippies were right, those people over 30 and traveling are usually pretty lonesome folks. Also it's harder to get a ride when you have a 30 year old dude standing next to you. Carry a small pocket knife, this knife is for eating and trimming your nails. If you ever feel threatened scream like a banshee and run away from the threat. If you can't run away run towards it. If somebody scares the shit out of you in a car and you don't like it, lock the strap of your seatbelt by pulling it towards the windshield quickly, try to control the brake pedal by applying slight pressure to decelerate the car as much as you can and pull the steering wheel a bit. You only want to do this if you are in fear for your life, somebody is taking you off the highway to a place you have clearly stated that you do not want to go and has exhibited violent behavior or language. If it doesn't wreck the car it'll freak out the driver enough to pull over, as soon as they pull over grab your shit and run towards the ditch. If there's no ditch stay where other motorists can see you and wave your arms, with the amount of cellphones nowadays someone is bound to call the cops and in this case they'll probably be on your side considering somebody tried to kill you by wrecking their own car. This is your story. If that is a little extreme what you can do is grab the wheel and slowly veer the car towards the emergency lane, however you might get an elbow to the face this way and end up jerking the wheel into a ditch and flipping the car. Which is what I did and I don't suggest it. When you are in a big city search out the poor neighborhoods and ask where the shelter is, that's where you'll find a shower and lunch. If you're especially hard up you can usually crash for a night or two but I always went for a shower and a shave and then found a good roof. Good roofs are everywhere downtown, especially near the manufacturing sector. A good roof is on top of a building that has no activity at night, and a building that has a fire escape. Wrap some para-chord around your shoe and throw the shoe at the bottom rung of the escape ladder. Hopefully you have enough chord so that when the shoe comes down you now have two ends of the chord and the bottom rung of the ladder in the middle. With both ends of the chord pull the ladder down, hold on to the ladder with one hand and put your shoe back on with the other. Now you have access to the safest fucking place to sleep ever. I used this trick in Seatle once and accidently broke into the new city records building. Also all skylights can be unscrewed with the back of your folding knife. Also don't ever break into a building, that's the only time where I almost ended up doing serious time. If I had been caught I would probably be sending this to you from prison. If you meet traveling performers on the road try and let them allow you to busk with them. Busking is street performance and you'll learn a lot of skills, also if you can cook these folk will really appreciate you because nobody wants to cook after a long day of work. Also these people can usually turn you on to traveling houses where if you are handy you can feed the residents and thus get free lodging for a week or two. This is how I traveled near the end of my journeys. I have built decks, roofs, even whole homes, wired these homes and plumbed them as well, but I have never been as appreciated as when I cooked for the people kind enough to have me. edit: Clarified the part on how to not get kidnapped. cont.

text: Some of us don't have lots of time to travel, but we still want to go places! We are a 30 something couple with two little kids. We want to go around the world and see as much as we can, but we are bound by our jobs and can't take big chunks of the year to go on long trips. Typically our trips are between 5 to 8 days. What happens often is that I ask for advice and am told that "X days is not enough to see place Y". And I get it, some of us can spend more time (and perhaps money) on travelling, spending weeks or months exploring the same place in depth. But others, like my family, cannot. I wish that the others understood those constraints better. We do not refer to our vacations as that, they are trips where we see much as we can. There is no lounging by a pool on our trips. Sure, we can't see all of Australia in a week there, but we can still explore a limited part of the country during that time. Same goes for our road trips within the U.S., which we do on a regular basis, easily driving 1,000 miles in a week going from place to place (flying into one airport and flying out of another). Sure we don't spend a week going on multiple hike in Zion, but we hit Zion for a couple days on a journey that also takes us to the Grand Canyon, Sedona, and Monument Valley! We do not want to miss the opportunity to travel the world while we are relatively young and follow the path of our parents who mostly denied themselves those opportunities until they retired. We strive for a middle ground for ourselves between becoming full-time travelers with remote work opportunities and dedicating our lives to our stable jobs well into your 50s and 60s. Again, this is just a rant! Enjoy your travels... I know I am itching to get back on an airplane to go to a new country and place as soon as we can. But I will only be there for a week!

text: Preparing to travel with pets is way harder than with babies!!! Let me just scream this into the void: PREPARING TO TRAVEL WITH PETS IS NOT EASIER THAN WITH A BABY. It is, in fact, a special kind of hell. I have traveled internationally with my cat, and every single time it's a stress-filled nightmare. And don't even get me started on domestic travel, we've lost flights and had reservations completely messed up because of a last-minute "policy change" that is nowhere to be found on their website. Dealing with the arbitrary, last-minute, "make-it-up-as-we-go" pet rules of airlines has made my anxiety while traveling so much worse. Let me paint you a picture of my suffering: Trip 1: Germany → Colombia (Pandemic Era) We were moving due to visa status and had to leave. Trying to call the airline to arrange our cat's travel was impossible because, surprise, COVID had every phone line blowing up. We showed up at the airport fully expecting to be left stranded. The only reason we weren't? The CAPTAIN of the plane took pity on us and saved our butts. We made it home, but my first gray hair was born that day. Trip 2: Colombia → Canada We check in, feeling smug because we're prepared. The agent looks at our tickets and says, "Oh, you booked a middle and window seat. Pets have to be in an aisle seat." Cue the frantic last-minute payment to switch seats. Mental note made: AISLE SEAT. Then, we landed during a ground crew strike. The trip took 10 hours total, and my fussy king DID NOT PEE ONCE. We were convinced his bladder was going to explode or he'd get a massive UTI. We were losing our minds. Trip 3: Canada → Colombia Learned my lesson, right? Booked an aisle and middle seat with the SAME AIRLINE. Walk up to the check-in counter, and the agent hits us with: "Actually, the pet carrier needs to be under the window seat. You need a window seat." ARE YOU KIDDING ME?! It's like they have a secret meeting to decide how to mess with me specifically. Every. Single. Time. It's something new. "Oh, this health certificate isn't quite right." "Oh, the carrier is half an inch too tall or too short." "Oh, we need to weigh him again, he looks heavy." It's always a surprise "gotcha!" Now I have a baby, and the preparation is basically: diapers, boobs (as she's ebf), a couple of onesies. Done. Meanwhile, for my two cats (yes, we got a second, I'm a masochist), it's a multi-month odyssey of vet appointments, government stamps, and anxiety. And the kicker? We can't even travel with the baby AND the cats at the same time. So yeah... our travel plans are on indefinite hold because of our furry overlords. And before anyone says, "JuSt LeAvE tHeM aT a PeT hOtEl," let me stop you right there. One of our cats is disabled. She can't pee or poop on her own and has to be expressed. She's my baby, THEY BOTH ARE MY BABIES. The thought of leaving them with strangers who may not understand their needs is a hard, resounding NO. Now we're planning a move to another country, and I'm already having panic attacks. We'll probably have to hire one of those expensive pet relocation agencies just to maintain our sanity. So, to conclude: Babies = Logistically Simple. Cats = A bureaucratic, unpredictable, soul-crushing ordeal. Thanks for coming to my TED Talk

text: overgeneralising after visiting a country. I travel regularly, mostly for work but also for fun, and read a lot country-specific and general travel subreddits. One particular thing which annoys me is that: Bad thing A happens in country B to person C who lives in country D Person C thinks this is country B specific thing (If C had the same incident at home D – which is possible – it would only be ”bad luck”) A few examples: A car rental experience: you are charged for a windshield crack which probably was there already before you got the car. One redditor had this experience in Switzerland and other in Iceland and they were shocked that how this can happen in such honest country. Yes, it can happen everywhere. It’s a classical ”legal scam” in the industry and it can happen also by accident, if the crack is small and previous rental guy misses it in rain or in dark. ”Germans are rude” no they are not, they just have a certain culture. I come from similar culture (Finland) and have never exceperienced the claimed rudeness as we have similar (not 100 % same but similar) ”rudeness”. Check the basics of the culture when visiting. In Finland you can say ”Beer!” to the bartender, in UK you say ”One beer, please.” And: of course there are individuals who are really assholes and if you have bad luck, you can meet one of them at your first day of the visit. ”I was pickpocketed in Iceland, I thought Iceland was safe” Places which attract tourists attract also pickpockets. If some country has low crime rate, it does not mean that there is no crime at all. Always mind your belongings. Of course there are country-specific things with risk level. It is a way easier to get pickpocketed in London than in Tokyo, but both are still possible. Same with car rental, it is easier to get a rock to windshield in Iceland than in Germany. But still, anything can happen everywhere. And people are people. edit: added a missing word
label: rant

text: Booked a $7/day rental car on Priceline. At the counter NU rental demanded proof of $300,000 liability insurance and wouldn't release the car without buying theirs. We booked a Priceline Express Deal for Tampa — $7/day. Priceline texted us after booking that the provider would be NU Car Rental. After a 20-minute wait at the airport, a shuttle picked us up along with three other parties and dropped us 6.5 miles away at what I can only describe as an office — a room not even 10x8, with three rental companies operating out of the same building, names I'd never heard of. At the counter everything started normal. We showed ID. Then the woman at the desk said we'd need to add insurance at $39/day. We said our own insurance covers it. She asked for proof, so we showed her the coverage on the insurer's website — she took a photo of the phone screen. Then she said, "this is not liability." Meanwhile the pressure started. "We close at 3pm, you have to decide faster." It was 2pm. She kept worrying about the next customer coming in. While we were deciding in the waiting area, another customer came out of the office — same story, he'd paid the extra $39/day. He had no choice, and he wasn't local. We went back and showed her our own policy covers liability. That's when she suddenly got specific: the liability has to be $300,000. We asked where that was written. Priceline's terms when you click agree just say you need to have liability — no amount. Nobody — not Priceline, not NU — told us $300,000 before we got to that room. So we asked her to show us where the $300,000 is written. She pulled out a printed terms sheet. It was for DFG Rent A Car. Not NU — a different company. (The sheet even lists Geico as an accepted insurer, and we had Geico.) That's when we looked at each other and walked out. Booked an Uber, we had a place to stay nearby, and later booked a car from Avis locally — no hassle at all. We let the ~$100 prepaid booking go. Turns out this isn't a one-off: BBB shows 53 complaints against NU Car Rental in 3 years, and Trustpilot reviews describe the exact same forced-insurance practice.

text: Ten day trip to Vietnam - HCMC, Ninh Binh, Hanoi. My partner and I just wrapped up a trip across Ho Chi Minh City, Ninh Binh, and Hanoi. We stayed in Airbnbs throughout, which gave us a lot of flexibility with our schedule and meals. We mostly explored on foot rather than relying on Grab. Walking around the neighborhoods—especially in Hanoi, which is bustling and endlessly interesting—is a great way to spend your time. Stopping for egg coffee or having a quiet evening cooking a simple meal at our Airbnb suited us best. We weren't planning to cover all the landmarks and just wanted to relax. At HCMC we visited a Buddhist temple and enjoyed their vegetarian pho as part of the community meal experience. We were welcomed warmly and offered the food. Google translate helped us have a lovely conversation too. A hands-on mother-of-pearl inlay workshop in Hanoi was one of our favorite activities. It was in the pedestrian area around Hoan Kiem lake. There were decent crowds and really good vibes. It was a great option to buy locally made arts and crafts for gifting. Other than that we kept market visits to a minimum and bought edible gifts like coffee, chocolate, and dried fruit from fixed-price shops. We tend to prefer cities, so Ninh Binh, though beautiful, was not my personal favorite part of the trip. Joining a group tour there turned out to be great value and a smooth experience overall. Climbing the Dragons peak was fun even with the crowd! We did our own cooking for the most part since we didn't want to worry about clarifying 'no fish sauce' in every meal. When we did eat out, we stuck strictly to dedicated vegetarian and vegan restaurants or stalls. A 40k VND bánh mì from a tiny vegan stall was my personal favorite! A few things to watch out for: pack warm layers and masks for this time of the year, just in case—we were both sick for a good chunk of our time in Hanoi due to an unexpected cold front, and the pollution likely contributed too. Check spa menu prices before walking in—some Old Quarter spas have high Google ratings alongside steep pricing. Check Green SM for much better airport drop prices than Grab. It was 100k vnd cheaper than Grab for us.
label: trip_report

text: TL;DR: I’ve been in Australia for 11 weeks, moved between several places and still haven’t found a stable job or a group of friends I really connect with. I’m slowly losing motivation and can feel my old depression and binge eating coming back. I’m not sure whether I should keep trying or go home. Hi everyone, I’m 24M and decided to move to Australia after finishing my vocational training in September 2025. Originally, I planned to fly here in March 2026. My main reasons were that I struggled to build close friendships in Germany. I wanted to meet new people, enjoy the warmer weather and hopefully build a new life in Australia, possibly staying for several years. Before leaving, I even tested what it was like to travel alone by spending a weekend in the Czech Republic. I realised that I could manage being alone, but what really mattered to me wasn’t where I was, but who I was surrounded by. Travelling alone felt quite boring. I always preferred having someone to share experiences with. Interestingly, a few weeks before my original flight, I developed a really close friendship in Germany. For the first time in years, I felt like I had a genuinely deep connection with someone again. Unfortunately, my flight was cancelled five days before departure because of the situation in Dubai, where I was supposed to have a stopover. I decided to postpone my trip until September so I could enjoy the German summer. During those months, I actually developed another two or three close friendships. So one of the main reasons I originally wanted to leave Germany had almost disappeared. Still, I decided to go. I thought I could only learn something from the experience, even if things didn’t go as planned. My first weeks in Australia: I spent my first five weeks with a family in Brisbane who made the start much easier for me. I didn’t have to work initially, so I had plenty of time to explore the city, meet new people through an app and edit the videos I had filmed. However, I still struggled with loneliness from time to time. Eventually, I met another German guy I got along with really well. We even decided to travel together. Unfortunately, on the same day, he received a job offer in Sydney and flew there. Since I didn’t have a clear plan for what I wanted to do in Australia, apart from meeting new people and completing the 88 days required for a possible second Working Holiday Visa, I initially focused on finding the right kind of work. Finding a job that counts towards those 88 days isn’t particularly easy. Eventually, I found a job on a watermelon farm near Tully, close to Cairns. My experience in Tully: It was a very small town, quite isolated from everything. Most backpackers lived in different shared houses around the area. I actually really enjoyed working on the watermelon farm, but I struggled with my free time. Everyone in my house had different working hours, so I barely saw the other people. Most of them also already knew each other and had their own groups of friends. There were parties, and I met people at work as well, but I never really connected with anyone. I got along with another person around my age, but she already had her own social circle and didn’t seem as interested in spending time together as I was. At some point, I even changed shared houses because I felt so lonely. However, my landlord put me in a house where I was completely alone, despite knowing how I was feeling. She told me that more people would move in the following week. On top of that, my MacBook broke, which was a big deal for me because I usually spent a lot of my free time editing videos and working on personal projects. Eventually, two acquaintances from Germany decided to fly to Sydney. Both were 19, and I had already met one of them a few times back in Germany. So I decided to leave Tully and join them in Sydney. Ironically, two days before my flight, I met a Dutch guy I got along with really well. Unfortunately, my flight was already booked, and I was also looking forward to Sydney. Now in Sydney: I’ve been in Sydney for around 10 days. I spent my first week in a hostel just a few minutes away from the two German guys. I imagined that we would spend a lot of time together, look for jobs and explore the city. However, they mostly do their own thing and seem quite happy without a third person. I also notice the age difference more than I expected. Since arriving, I’ve been looking for work every single day. I walk around the city handing out my CV, apply online and approach different employers. I have several qualifications, including RSA, RSG and a White Card. So far, I’ve had two trial shifts at different restaurants, but I still haven’t managed to find a permanent job. It’s becoming increasingly frustrating. I’ve completed two vocational training programmes in Germany and worked several different jobs, yet sometimes I feel like I’m worth nothing in the Australian job market. At the same time, I’ve been trying to meet other backpackers through my hostel and an app. I met one girl I got along with really well, but once again, she already had her own social circle and didn’t seem particularly interested in making new connections. A few days ago, I moved from the hostel into an Airbnb. Unfortunately, that turned out to be a bad decision. It’s about an hour away from the city centre, quite isolated, and there aren’t really any people my age around. Next Saturday, I’ll finally move into a shared house in central Sydney with the two German guys. Until then, I’m trying to keep myself busy. I go to the gym regularly, meet other backpackers, apply for jobs, edit videos on my phone and read. But despite all of this, my mood keeps getting worse. Yesterday, I went out for dinner with the two German guys. Normally, I really enjoy going out for food, but even that felt boring. It made me realise that I currently don’t really have anything I’m looking forward to in Australia. I can feel my old depression slowly coming back. I’ve also noticed my binge eating episodes returning. Some days are better than others, but I can definitely feel a change in my mental health. I do have coping strategies that helped me in the past, and I’m trying to use them. However, I feel like I’m missing many of the things that normally keep me mentally stable: close friendships, a regular job, my MacBook and even access to nature, like a forest where I can go for a walk. What should I do? I’ve started seriously thinking about flying back to Germany, but I’m incredibly unsure. It’s winter there now, and I’m afraid I might regret leaving. After all, I could find a job tomorrow, meet someone I really connect with next week or finally find the group of friends I’ve been looking for. On the other hand, I’m slowly losing hope. I know that 11 weeks isn’t necessarily a long time, and I don’t expect everything to fall into place immediately. But I’ve put so much energy into meeting people, finding work and building a life here, and I feel like I’m getting nowhere. I’m not necessarily looking for someone to tell me whether I should stay or go home. I’d genuinely appreciate some honest advice from people who have experienced something similar. Have you ever felt this way while travelling or living abroad? What helped you get through it? And how did you know when it was time to move on or go home?
label: question

text: 6 hours around Ciudad del Este in Paraguay. Having visited Iguazu Falls, it felt like a missed opportunity not to hop over the (triple) border into neighbouring Paraguay. So, starting in Argentinian Puerto Iguazu, we got on the Rio Uruguay bus and crossed into Brazil, and then into Paraguay - interestingly, stopping for passport control only once, leaving Argentina. Same on the way back, entering Argentina. Main attractions were definitely Monday Falls and the Itaipu Dam, where we joined a free tour. The Falls were incomparably smaller than Iguazu, but refreshingly less touristy, while the dam proved a true engineering marvel, spectacularly massive, covering 90% of the electricity needs of the country of Paraguay. The little that we saw of the actual city center of Ciudad del Este can be described as beautifully chaotic, but not unlike many other small cities in the region or indeed even in Southeast Asia. In this case, due to its border location, it was primarily focused on the shopping experience. Photos: 1-2 Monday Falls 3-6 Itaipu Dam 7-11 Ciudad del Este city center

text: If you’re planning a cruise and want to protect yourself against something like the recent FAA ground stop, I’d strongly recommend purchasing a separate travel insurance policy that specifically covers air traffic control disruptions, missed connections and trip interruption. One company I’d look at is Seven Corners. Some of their travel protection plans include coverage for common carrier delays and certain air traffic control shutdowns. The important thing is to make sure the policy would cover the cost of catching up with your cruise at another port, additional airfare, hotels and potentially the nonrefundable cruise cost if you can’t make the sailing. These benefits have specific conditions and limits, and not every FAA ground stop will qualify. Here’s their website: https://www.sevencorners.com I’d also compare policies at https://www.insuremytrip.com and specifically ask whether an FAA computer or communications outage that grounds flights would be considered a covered reason for missing your cruise. I wouldn’t rely solely on Cancel For Any Reason insurance because most CFAR policies require you to cancel at least 48 hours before departure, which wouldn’t help much with an unexpected ground stop the morning of your flight. And regardless of the insurance, I’d strongly recommend flying into your cruise departure city at least one or two days early, especially for an international cruise. That extra day could save you thousands of dollars and a lot of aggravation.
label: advice

Unfortunately it's filled with con artists who are just trying to steal your money with bs stories. I lost track of the number of people who 'stamped my passport at the airport' or 'am raising money for the under 16s basketball team'. Monument to the German colonial times in Apia. Found this random satellite station on a peninsula outside Apia. No idea what it's for, but it was a highlight. Robert Louis Stevenson's house, Samoa. Bit of a hike to get there, but apparently seeing his grave at the top of the mountain is even harder. Nuku'alofa is Tonga's main city. It's full of stray dogs - the locals carry sticks to scare them off as people do get bitten. Nobody mentions that on Sunday everything is closed except the Chinese restaurant (by law). Tongans were very friendly and very chill in my experience, but I wasn't a fan of the island's habit of ringing every bell at 5am to say thanks to Jesus. Sun up in Tonga. text: Sri Lanka. We spent almost two weeks traveling around Sri Lanka, starting on the southwest coast before heading inland to Ella and Kandy and finishing in Colombo. We stayed roughly 2–3 days in each place. Overall, it was an incredible adventure, though definitely a mixed experience in some ways. What we loved Nature. Easily the island’s biggest draw. Even after researching the trip beforehand I wasn’t prepared for just HOW MUCH wildlife and natural diversity we’d see everywhere. Animals I’d only ever seen in books or zoos were casually wandering around town, let alone out in the countryside. So many fascinating birds and plants, so much color. Almost any view in Sri Lanka is beautiful by default. Beaches. Beautiful, tropical, sandy beaches. We got lucky with a cleaner private beach at our first hotel, with no rocks, but most of the beaches we saw looked like lovely places to spend time. The only catch was the constant waves. We didn’t have a single calm day by the sea, though if you’re into surfing, that might be a bonus (we didn’t try it) Food. I was surprised by the variety of vegetarian dishes and how creatively fruit was used. I’m usually someone who wants meat with a meal, but I kept trying vegan dishes here and really enjoying them. Buses and tuk-tuks. I loved how much personality people gave their vehicles. Every bus was a ridiculously colorful work of art, covered in hilariously cheesy stickers saying things like “Turbo Charged Edition,” “ADIDAS,” and so on. It was quite funny and charming overall. What we didn’t enjoy Getting around on foot. Before the trip I saved loads of sights on Google Maps imagining we’d stroll around towns and take in the local culture. That feels pretty funny in hindsight. In practice, most places we visited barely had any sidewalks so walking meant squeezing along the roadside beside smelly diesel buses and endless tuk-tuks whose drivers seemed determined to kill both each other and us. Somehow, a two-lane road becomes four or even five lanes, and there’s definitely no room left for pedestrians. Persistent sales pitches. To be clear, I mean people selling things or services to tourists -drivers, restaurant staff, etc. rather than people in general. But if you’re visibly a white tourist, tuk-tuks will constantly pull up beside you offering rides and tours, often refusing to take a simple no for an answer. Someone is always trying to lead you somewhere, get you into a shop, or sell you something at a wildly inflated price. It gets exhausting, especially combined with the traffic situation above. Going for a simple walk around any town started to feel like a test of mental endurance. Extra charges at restaurants. Quite a few places listed prices without taxes, then added a service charge on top. I hate this kind of pricing. Just show me what I’m actually going to pay instead of making me do the math. Litter. Unfortunately, we saw whole piles of rubbish along the coast and roadsides sometimes. In some coastal areas, people piled it up and burned it. It was awful to see, though the lack of public bins made part of the problem understandable. Even in Colombo, the biggest city, we could barely find any ways to get rid of thrash. Sometimes I’d finish a bottle of water and carry it around for another hour before finally throwing it away back at the hotel room. Service. Service was often painfully slow. We usually had to flag someone down to get a menu, have dirty plates cleared, or order anything. Even a glass of water could take 15 minutes or more. And apparently napkins are worth their weight in gold here, lol. By the end of the trip, my wife and I had a running joke about how many napkins per person we’d get at the next café. Usually zero or one. Entrance fees at major sights. I understand charging tourists to support the economy and maintain these places. Still, some tickets felt expensive. Sigiriya, for example—the famous Lion Rock fortress—was $35 per person, before transport, a guide, or anything else. Overall thoughts Despite the long list of negatives, I came away feeling much more positive than negative about the trip. The downsides are real, but the highlights are so spectacular that they’re worth experiencing firsthand. My biggest regret is planning too much time around staying in towns and walking around them, which ended up being the least enjoyable part. Lounging on a beach or hiking through the hills and jungle was so much better - those were the moments when Sri Lanka really shined. If I were planning the trip again I’d focus much more on national parks, tea plantations, Sinharaja rainforest maybe, beach time, and drinking coconut cocktails

text: Smartfares booking. I stupidly booked flights from Norway to Zanzibar with Smartfares. I say "stupidly" because I'm always advising people to book hotels and transport directly with the provider rather than third party websites but for some reason in this instance I used a middleman. I don't consider Smartfares a scam but my experience was not great. I booked return flights in one session. Leaving Norway at 6am, to arrive at Copenhagen 7am. Onward to Istanbul 11am and then on to Zanzibar. After booking the tickets were sent to me the following day. After another day the booking appeared on the Turkish airlines site and then a week later they showed up on the SAS website. All good, we're going to Zanzibar. 3 weeks before travel I looked in on the SAS website. The flight from Norway has disappeared (must have been cancelled) and I'd been rebooked going out from Norway at 2pm, arriving CPH 3pm - to catch the connection at 11am... Clearly not gonna work. I emailed Smartfares, who to their credit called me the next day, admittedly at 4am. Not sure where they called from but the guy had difficulty understanding my proposed solution which was to travel to CPH the afternoon the day before so we could overnight in CPH and catch the scheduled flights the next day. They changed the first leg of the journey at an extra cost of $400. Plus of course I had to pay for the airport hotel. What's scary is that neither SAS, Turkish airlines or Smartfares seemed to be aware that the change in schedule would have ruined the entire trip and it was only noticed because I checked myself. My question here is: do I have any possibility of claiming back the flight price difference and the hotel cost? If so then how do I go about that? Ultimately I can do a chargeback for the flights but not for the hotel. Anyone got any ideas?

text: My thoughts and advice on the rental cars. OK, this is probably a bunch of stuff that a whole lot of people already know but I’m just inclined to tell you my thoughts now. Just spent about an hour dealing with Avis. I returned the car completely full but because there was nobody checking the cars in, I just had to leave the car in a return lane. I returned it completely filled but they charged me $85 for 8 gallons of gas. The only reason I didn’t get charged ultimately was I had a picture of the gas receipt and I took a picture of the dashboard when I returned it. Still a massive pain in the ass contacting them, but I got the fee finally reversed. Payless did the same thing to me last year. Same situation, nobody checking the car in, I returned it full and they charge me close to $100. Again it was just having pictures of the gas receipt and the dashboard upon return that got me out of it. Five years ago, I hit a wall backing up when we had a rental in Portugal. Charged us about €600 at the time to fix it. Because I had rented it with the Credit Card I had to jump through the hoops but the Credit Card company ultimately paid for the damages. Two years after that Hertz charged me €1200 for some kind of damage that I didn’t understand to the rental car in France. Same Credit Card covered us for all of the damages. Avis also told me the only car that I could take was a giant Chevy Silverado with my last rental even though I had just rented a compact car. I looked it up and sure enough, the Credit Card company, in their list of terms, said they would not cover the Silverado or other cars similar to that. So that’s it. Running a car just kinda sucks now but freaking pay attention to all of your paperwork and keep everything. And for the love of God take pictures of your dashboard when you get the car and when you return the car. Actually just videotape the whole car when you get it. And the hell with Avis and Payless And yay for the Capital One credit cards. They’ve been really awesome with how they’ve handled these issues with rental cars.
label: advice

text: My 10 day experience in Dubai - some tips for anyone interested. We stayed closer to the creek up north on purpose - so we could reach old Dubai and Deira more easily. Plus it took only 15-20min to Downtown, 25 to Marina area by car. My tip is to stay somewhere between Downtown and Deira on the red metro line. That way you'll get to the most interesting parts of Dubai relatively easy and cheaper. I hated Marina, it was like a huge resort built just for vacation. To each their own but you will get poor very fast here. Restaurants were expensive and somehow the vibe was very not culturally accurate. Cheesecake factory, Tim Horton's etc you get the point. Like an American village. Skip the popular tourist malls - Dubai Mall is undoubtedly incredible and worth seeing because whatever you imagine it has shopping wise make it ten times more. It has EVERY brand on earth but you will probably end up window shopping because the brands are also high end. What I suggest you do is find the smaller, further away malls where normal locals go. You find a more varied selection of shops and much better deals and shopping. For example Deira has many fun, mid size malls worth exploring. The Dubai Outlet mall is a 25min ride but is larg with great deals! I was disappointed with the souks, mostly because they seemed to cater tourists. Both traditional and mall versions. Al seef was such a waste of time imho. Sure the Gold souk is interesting if you want to buy gold (21k is best for wear, 24k for a coin/bar, as we were told). Meena bazaar has a fun Little India vibe that is worth seeing in the evening! Karama is another fun one. If you want cheap food, go to Karama or Deira. Indian food is so goddamn cheap and delicious here. Like, mind blowingly cheap. You will easily eat with less than $5 a meal+drink. Coffee can be vvvvvvery expensive, at least to my taste. If you sit down at a regular looking cafe an americano can cost you easily $5, not to mention all the delicious specialty drinks. A cafe cake from $10 onwards. Chai and karak are their own thing, cheap af. But do splurge on pistachio milk cake! Taxis are not as cheap as one would think. The distances are so long you end up paying maybe $30-50 a day on them. Metro is fine, just takes a long time. Walking to and from the stations takes a long time as well. From Burj Khalifa M to Dubai mall is like, 1-2km. If you look at the map and think you'll just cross the road, nope, think again. Sheikh Zayed has 12-14 lanes total. The detour of finding a crossing can eat up 45-60min. Walking to places is simply not possible. You need to know where you want to go. The kind of wander off and explore thing seemed very much impossible. Talk about walking, you will end up doing it still quite a lot so truly take good shoes with you. You will spend most of your time indoors unless you are by the pool or beach, because the heat is quite something. Best time to visit starts at the end of November. A light blouse is a good way to cover up respecting the culture and you will find very nice, airy and breathable clothes at malls. Locals dress very neat and conservative, so I think that is something to consider. The city is filled with immigrants. I think it said somewhere that only 15-20% are Emirati. The stories we heard from drivers and hospitality workers were heartwrenching. To think you are working 4-6m at a time before you get to go home and see your children is tough. Living with 2-6 other workers.... Everyone I met was an immigrant working their asses off to provide for 1-3 familied back home. The city is not Emirati, but a hub of Asians. If it were a democracy it would probably have an Indian/Pakistani government lol. And that brings to my best point about Dubai - the food here is sublimely versatile and good! If you want Filipino food, its good. Singaporean, good. Indian, good. Lebanese, good. You get my point. Go to Dubai to eat. Skip the touristy shit and let your taste buds lead the way. That is probably the only way to truly enjoy this city if you are not a millionaire. If I ever come back it's to enjoy the sunny weather and Indian food without going all the way to India. The city has nice boardwalks here and there, so do explore beyond Marina and other tourist hubs. Ask away, I had many thoughts throughout my stay and didn't write them all down. Ask about any shopping you are thinking of doing in Dubai, I can try to give some idea if its worth it.

Is Barcelona or Madrid better for NYE as a solo traveler? If this route is a bad idea, how would you route these last 9 days? label: question

text: I personally wouldn't do three cities in 9 days-- especially in 2 countries. Barcelona and Madrid are a relatively easy and direct train ride away from one another, but Budapest to Spain means a flight, which will eat up a big chunk of time and energy. Also, since it's winter, weather could impact flights. Fwiw, every country you've mentioned here... Germany, Czech, Hungary and Spain are full of amazing cities and towns outside of their largest cities and could easily fill 2 weeks or more just exploring within each country. If it were me, especially during winter, I'd pick one or two bases and then take some day trips from there. In terms of "better" for NYE.... Madrid has a significantly more Spanish vibe than Barcelona and tends to be more festive and lit up in a traditionally winter holiday type way. But, Barcelona parties harder. I'm the kind that strongly prefers the former, but it depends on your personality and what you're looking for. The route between Lisbon and Madrid actually isn't that quick, it would be a flight. You'd be much better off sticking with Spain and either doing day trips from Madrid (Toledo, Segovia, etc....) or visiting another Spanish city like Valencia.
label: advice

text: Sharing one “special” thing we try to do when traveling, hope it inspires a few people. We try to find a local cooking class when we travel to new places. Not only is it a fun activity to do, but often times it comes with a half day or so of hanging out and drinking some wine while learning how to cook a new cultures cuisine. This is also something we “take back” with us and end up using new techniques, recipes, or flavor profiles when we cook at home. We are in no way part of the food industry, though I worked in kitchens as a cook for years when I was younger. Our top experience so far was we had a cooking class in Barcelona where, as part of the class, they took us to the huge food market, introduced us to vendors personally, tested and sampled all types of food for hours while shopping and learning, then went back and cooked a multi course full meal with two other couples, and drank wine for hours. It is one of our top travel memories. Sharing this as I hope it inspires others to try it out. It’s such an awesome thing to bring people together with food throughout the world, and it’s always been an exceptional experience.

text: How to deal with jet lag in a 1 day layover. When I booked it, I didn't think much about the fact I would be almost 24 hours in Hawaii, or that it could be nice to check out Honolulu on the way to Japan. But now I am worried about how to deal with jet lag or if the flights would be too tiring. Jet lag between the U.S. East Coast and Japan is likely hard enough, and throwing a day in a third timezone is probably going to confuse my body and disrupt my sleep even more. This would be my first time traveling such a long distance. Do you think this layover is doable? When thinking about solutions, I thought maybe for the layover, I can pretend I am still in America and go to sleep early (7 or 8 pm), shortly after the sun sets. Then I wake up very early (relative to Hawaii), expose myself to light as if it was already morning, see the sun rise, and get going to Japan and then suffer the jetlag as if I only had one flight. I am not sure how feasible this is. text: Airplane seat courtesy rules. Traveling recently, had a lady sitting already in my assigned seat. I pointed it out when I got to my row and she said, "Oh, you can't trade with me?" Then gestured to the middle seat. I told her no, and she shrugged and moved saying that it didn't cost anything to ask. My problem wasn't with her asking, but with sitting in my seat and then assuming I would be too uncomfortable to make her move. It felt manipulative, like if I was more afraid of confrontation, she could have made me switch. Am I overthinking? Too sensitive? My personal opinion is one can definitely ask but remain in your assigned and paid for seat until you have a chance to ask the person. Thoughts on if this is rude, normal, or other? EDIT FOR CLARITY: I saw someone post how they switched their seat and got snacks from that person. In spite of not switching with this older lady, she did offer me multiple snacks which I politely declined (I'm quite germ aware, especially on planes) and she was pleasant and chatted with the lady in the aisle seat like they were besties, even though Im pretty sure they didnt know each other. Im sure it was a tactic she thought she'd use like how some people bring treats for the airline workers hoping for free upgrades, and I genuinely don't think she saw anything wrong with what she did. I just wanted for a lot of people to see this because I used to be way more of a people pleaser than I am now, and some people may do this exact thing thinking its harmless when its really a manipulative tactic. I'm of the opinion that it is still okay to ask nicely and make sure its as pressure free as possible but to sit in the wrong seat on purpose is the main issue and if you do this, please stop it

text: Copenhagen/Sjaelland Trip Report. Like my last post, this is from a trip that happened a while ago. I visited Copenhagen and the surrounding areas over Labor Day weekend in 2022, arriving on Friday, and leaving on Tuesday, my shortest trip overseas to date. Photos: 1-2: Grounds of Fredriksborg Palace (Hillerod) 3: Kronborg (Helsingor) 4: Canal near Christiansborg Palace 5: Marble Church 6-7: Views from the ramparts of the Kastellet 8-10: Ponds/Lakes found in Copenhagen 11: Rosenborg 12: Reverse of Elephant Tower 13: Nyhavn 14: Panorama from Vor Frelsers Kirke 15: Borsen (Unfortunately burned down in 2024) 16: View of Cathedral and Bishop's Palace (Roskilde) (I somehow forgor to add this one :'( ) Pros: Copenhagen and Denmark were orderly and calm during my time there. A welcome change of pace to the chaos I had been used to as someone who had been raised in the NY metro area, and had only been to Portugal and China up to that point. People crossed the street when the light was green, the bikers adhered strictly to rules and norms, and drivers did not seem to do their utmost to inconvenience others just so they might save 30 seconds on their commute. There was ample green space in the city, providing plenty of places where one could sit, relax, and forget that they were sitting within a European capital city. Families could be found in abundance having picnics, going on walks, or simply laying in the grass. Copenhagen was also extremely clean. It is not particularly something I prioritize when traveling, but I certainly welcomed not being nasally assaulted by aromas which reminded me of eating 15 feet from a pigsty whilst visiting my grandma during my youth. Cons: The only con I personally saw in Copenhagen was the cost of living. For me, being from New York, it was relatively similar to what I am used to. But I understand that for others, especially those visiting from outside of Europe, where airfare adds considerably to the cost of a trip, paying 40 dollars for a meal at a perfectly standard, not at all upscale restaurant, can be prohibitive. Highlights: Hot dogs in Nordic countries are marvelous, and sustained me throughout my trip. Unfortunately, I did not take the opportunity to properly sit down and eat in any restaurants, besides a Chinese restaurant near to the main train station, but I take solace in knowing that the glizzies are good enough to live on for 4 days. Day trips to Roskilde for its historic cathedral, Hillerod for its Fredriksborg Palace, and Helsingor for Kronborg (Hamlet's very own castle), are very highly recommended. The public transit in Sjaelland is very straightforward, and there are actually a good amount of interconnections which make doing multiple trips in a day very feasible. The areas of Christianshavn, and Fredriksberg were both fairly quiet and relaxed in my experience. Whilst being in walking distance of the city center, where most of the sights were, the vibes of the respective areas were very different, with Christianshavn seemingly being an area where people in their 20's and 30's went to spend an afternoon or meet with friends for drinks or dinner, and Fredriksberg seeming to be a more family friendly neighborhood. All of these photos were taken on an iPhone 7, please don't be harsh if they are bad

text: Here is a brain dump of why Milledgeville, GA is the most Southern Gothic city. (Although, Savannah and Charleston have their own claims) Milledgeville, hometown of Flannery O’Connor, the Southern Gothic writer. She grew up and died here. The Old Capital of GA, home to the Old Governors mansion and the legislative chambers- which is done in a gothic architecture, restored and has the legislators desks, gallery for viewers. At one time the city was Home of the worlds largest insane asylum, now its campus of thousands of acres of land sit empty. A plot of land with small metal stakes with numbers, each assigned to a different patient. In the 80’s a yard crew pulled them all up to cut the grass because they thought it would be easier and now there is no record of who and where. There has been great effort to re-establish the cemetery. Over 25,000 patients were committed to the hospital at its highest occupancy. Thousands and thousands dropped off and forgotten A museum is now located in Central State Hospital’s train depot. They had a dedicated train line. There used to be an old southern threat that “I’m going to send you to Milledgeville” which meant that you had gone “crazy”. The other saying was when men started to tire of their wives they would “49 ‘em” which meant they would commit them to the hospital by driving on Hwy 49. The people that remember and lived in this world would be in their 80’s now. A thriving liberal arts college campus sits on the land that was known as penitentiary square prior to 1880’s. The executions occurred there for the state. The capital from 1803 until the end of the civil war. Sherman came through but didn’t burn the town. Local legend is that Sherman had a mistress in Monticello, GA and she asked him to spare the city because she had family here. Sherman trashed the legislature chambers, raided the armory, slept in the governors mansion, stabled his horses inside the episcopal church and poured molasses in the organ pipes but he didn’t light a single match The novel Paris Trout was set in Milledgeville and based on a true story about Marion Wilson, who committed mass murder during the 150 anniversary parade. He shot 5 people, killing 3 attorneys and then themself in the second story of the downtown theater, while the marching band went by and a float of waving high school girls were happy because they were who sold the most tickets to the sesquicentennial dance that night. There never was a dance. There is Memory Hill cemetery where Flannery rests that is also home to a witch they hung but no one would touch her so they dug a hole under her and waited for her to “fall in on her own”. Wild Bill Hitchcock is supposed to be buried here after a life as a train robber. There is the grave of a family surrounded on all sides by chain, that is broken in the front. It is where a black family, the Simmons, a family who still owns their great-great-great grandfathers commercial properties, was born into slavery, opened a business and bought a plot in the “white cemetery” and had the chains there to remind everyone. This is Creek Indian country and was not part of Georgia when it was scouted to be the capital of GA. It is one of a few planned capital cities. The roads are a grid, nice, large homes were built by the very best architects at the time, like John Marlor. There is even a Milledgeville federal style of architecture
